text: You are deciding which tools to give a code-review agent that must read source, search the repository, and leave review comments - but must never modify files. Which toolset selection follows the module's guidance?

options.text: Grant the full default toolset; the agent's instructions tell it not to write.
options.why: Instructions are guidance. A capability the agent holds is a capability it can use, and tool allowlists are the enforcement layer.

options.text: Grant a read-only toolset plus the specific comment capability, and nothing else.
options.why: The capability boundary should match the job: read-only toolsets for planning and review agents, implementation tools reserved for execution agents. Prefer allowlists over broad wildcards, and treat changes to the allowlist as a governance-sensitive change.

options.text: Grant read plus write, since review agents occasionally need to fix trivial typos.
options.why: "Occasionally needs" is how scope creep starts. If typo fixing is in scope, that is a different agent with a different, deliberately granted capability.

options.text: Grant no tools and paste the diff into the prompt manually.
options.why: This removes the agent's ability to gather its own context and does not scale. Least privilege means the minimum needed, not zero.

takeaway: Identify tools from the task's actual verbs, then allowlist exactly those. Read-only for planning and review; write tools for execution agents only.

text: Agent profile configuration provides three kinds of control. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Capability boundary = which tools are allowed; visibility boundary = whether the agent is user-selectable; delegation boundary = which subagents can be invoked.
options.why: These are the three controls the operations unit names. Capability governs tools, visibility governs whether a human can pick the agent in interactive UI, and delegation governs which subagents it may hand off to.

options.text: Capability boundary = the model used; visibility boundary = log verbosity; delegation boundary = runner size.
options.why: None of these are governance boundaries. Model, logging, and runner sizing are operational settings.

options.text: Capability boundary = branch protection; visibility boundary = repository visibility; delegation boundary = CODEOWNERS.
options.why: These are repository controls, not agent-profile controls. They act on the change after it exists, not on what the agent may do.

options.text: Capability boundary = token scope; visibility boundary = artifact retention; delegation boundary = concurrency group.
options.why: Token scope is related but is a workflow permission concern; retention and concurrency are unrelated to agent-profile boundaries.

takeaway: Agent profiles set three boundaries: capability (tools), visibility (user-selectable or not), and delegation (which subagents can be invoked).

text: You want a custom agent that only looks at JavaScript files and the src/auth/ tree, and can only read and search. Where and how do you express that?

options.text: In a .agent.md file under .github/agents/, using applyTo for the file scope and tools for the allowed actions.
options.why: Custom agents live in .github/agents/ with the .agent.md extension. applyTo narrows which files or directories the agent focuses on and tools defines what actions it can perform - for example read_file and search_files.

options.text: In .github/workflows/agent.yml, using a paths filter on the trigger.
options.why: A paths filter decides whether a workflow runs at all. It does not scope what an agent may touch once it is running.

options.text: In CODEOWNERS, by assigning the agent as owner of those paths.
options.why: CODEOWNERS routes review requests to owners; it grants and restricts nothing at execution time.

options.text: In the repository's Copilot settings, by listing allowed directories.
options.why: Repository settings enable the cloud agent for the repository. Within-repository focus is refined in the agent file.

takeaway: Repository scope defines where an agent operates; the custom agent file (applyTo, tools) defines what it may access and do inside that boundary.

text: A workflow's analysis job only reads code, but a later job must open a pull request. Which permissions layout is correct?

options.text: Set permissions: write-all at workflow level so neither job can fail on a permission error.
options.why: This grants every job far more than it needs and is the "excess permissions" anti-pattern: a small mistake in the read-only job becomes a repository-wide incident.

options.text: Set contents: read at workflow level, then grant contents: write and pull-requests: write on the job that writes.
options.why: Read-only defaults at workflow level with job-level elevation is the published least-privilege pattern. Only the job that must write gets write capability, so the blast radius of the analysis job stays minimal.

options.text: Omit the permissions block entirely and rely on repository defaults.
options.why: Defaults vary by repository and organization settings. The guidance is to define permissions explicitly and minimize them.

options.text: Store a personal access token as a secret and use it in both jobs.
options.why: A PAT carries the user's broad access and bypasses the per-run scoping that GITHUB_TOKEN provides. It is a wider blast radius, not a narrower one.

takeaway: Default to read at workflow level; elevate write only on the specific job that needs it. pull-requests: write is an elevated capability.

text: In VS Code, you are adding the GitHub remote MCP server to an agent. Which sequence matches the documented flow?

options.text: Edit .github/workflows/mcp.yml and add the server URL under tools.
options.why: That is workflow configuration, not the IDE flow. MCP servers are added through the Copilot Chat interface and become tools the agent can use.

options.text: Open Copilot Chat in Agent mode, choose Configure tools, Add MCP server, select HTTP, enter https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, pick a scope, then authenticate and save.
options.why: This is the documented VS Code flow: the Tools icon, Configure tools, Add MCP server, HTTP server type, the server URL, a workspace or all-workspaces scope, then Authenticate and Save. The server then appears as a tool the agent can call.

options.text: Install the server as a GitHub App from the Marketplace and grant it repository access.
options.why: GitHub Apps are a different integration model. MCP servers are registered as tools for the client, not installed as apps on the repository.

options.text: Add the server to CODEOWNERS so the agent is authorized to call it.
options.why: CODEOWNERS has no relationship to tool authorization.

takeaway: MCP servers are added through the client (Copilot Chat, Agent mode, Configure tools) and become callable tools; remote is the recommended setup for most users.

text: A developer needs an MCP server that can reach files on their own machine and a bespoke internal script. Which configuration fits, and what changes?

options.text: A remote server, because remote is always recommended.
options.why: Remote is recommended for most users of the GitHub MCP server, but it cannot reach local resources. The recommendation is a default, not a rule.

options.text: A local server pointed at something like http://localhost:3000; setup in VS Code is otherwise identical and it typically needs no external authentication.
options.why: Local MCP servers run on the developer's machine, can access local resources and custom workflows, and typically require no external authentication. The VS Code setup steps are the same - only the endpoint differs.

options.text: A remote server with a firewall exception for the developer's machine.
options.why: Inverting the direction does not help. A hosted server still does not have the local filesystem.

options.text: Neither - MCP cannot expose local resources.
options.why: Bridging to local resources is one of the documented capabilities of a local MCP server.

takeaway: Local MCP servers reach local resources and usually skip external auth; remote servers reduce setup and travel across environments.

text: Which statement about MCP server hosting options across GitHub deployments is accurate?

options.text: GitHub Enterprise Server supports local MCP server configuration, while GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency supports both local and remote.
options.why: This is the documented split. Deployment model constrains which hosting options are available, so it is worth checking before you standardize on remote.

options.text: Remote MCP servers are the only supported option on every GitHub deployment.
options.why: Local configuration is supported, and on GitHub Enterprise Server it is the supported path.

options.text: Local MCP servers are only supported in GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
options.why: This reverses the actual situation for GitHub Enterprise Server.

options.text: MCP server hosting is identical across all GitHub deployments.
options.why: Support differs by deployment, which is exactly why the modules call it out.

takeaway: Check the deployment: Enterprise Server supports local configuration; Enterprise Cloud with data residency supports both local and remote.

text: Your enterprise is hosting a custom MCP registry for Copilot. Which requirements must it satisfy? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Follow the MCP registry v0.1 specification
options.why: Yes. The registry must conform to the specification for Copilot to consume it.

options.text: Expose HTTPS endpoints including GET /v0.1/servers and the per-server version endpoints
options.why: Yes - GET /v0.1/servers, GET /v0.1/servers/{serverName}/versions/latest, and GET /v0.1/servers/{serverName}/versions/{version}.

options.text: Include CORS headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers
options.why: Yes. Without the required CORS headers Copilot cannot access the registry from the client.

options.text: Be hosted inside the same repository as the agent that consumes it
options.why: No. A registry is an org- or enterprise-level service. You can fork and self-host the open-source registry, run it locally with Docker, build your own, or use Azure API Center as a managed registry.

takeaway: A custom registry needs the v0.1 spec, the three HTTPS endpoints, and CORS headers - then the registry URL goes into Copilot policy settings.

text: An enterprise sets Restrict MCP access to registry servers to "Registry only". A developer's local MCP server stops working. Why, and what fixes it?

options.text: Local servers are always exempt from the policy; the failure must be a network issue.
options.why: Local servers are not exempt. Under Registry only, they must be listed in the registry too.

options.text: Under Registry only, local servers must also be listed in the registry, with server IDs matching exactly.
options.why: That is the documented behavior. Registry only limits developers to servers defined in the configured registry, and local MCP servers must be included with exactly matching server IDs.

options.text: The developer must switch to Allow all in their personal Copilot settings.
options.why: The policy is set at organization or enterprise level and applies immediately to all developers. Individuals cannot override it.

options.text: Local servers require a paid Copilot seat upgrade under Registry only.
options.why: Allowlist enforcement is tied to the Copilot seat that governs the user, but the fix here is registry listing, not a seat change.

takeaway: "Allow all" means any server; "Registry only" means registry-listed servers only - including local ones, with exactly matching IDs.

text: MCP servers, registries, and allow lists each solve a different part of the same problem. Which mapping is correct?

options.text: Server exposes tools; registry makes servers discoverable and trustable; allow list decides which servers are permitted.
options.why: This is the three-part model the module summarizes. Together they let teams discover useful servers while the organization keeps governance over what is actually allowed.

options.text: Server decides what is permitted; registry exposes tools; allow list makes servers discoverable.
options.why: The roles are shuffled. Permission is policy (allow list), discovery is catalog (registry), and exposure is the server.

options.text: Registry enforces read/write permissions; allow list exposes tools; server catalogs available clients.
options.why: None of these are the documented responsibilities. A registry is a catalog, not a permission engine.

options.text: All three are alternative names for the same organization policy setting.
options.why: They are three distinct components, configured in different places.

takeaway: Server = exposes tools. Registry = discovery and distribution. Allow list = the policy gate.

text: Which elements make up an agent's execution context in GitHub? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The repository the agent is working in
options.why: Yes. Repository scope is the first boundary; agents cannot reach other repositories unless explicitly granted.

options.text: The branch the agent is targeting
options.why: Yes. Branch-based isolation keeps changes off the default branch until review.

options.text: The workflow executing the tasks and the permissions granted to it
options.why: Yes. The workflow is the controlled execution container and its permissions determine capability.

options.text: The number of contributors with write access to the repository
options.why: No. Contributor count has no bearing on what an agent may do; capability comes from permissions, not from headcount.

takeaway: Execution context = repository + branch + workflow + permissions. Together they determine both visibility and capability.

text: Where do you enable and scope the Copilot cloud agent for a single repository?

options.text: Organization settings, Copilot, Policies - then list the repository.
options.why: Organization Copilot policies govern features such as MCP usage across the org. Enabling the cloud agent for a specific repository is a repository-level action.

options.text: Repository Settings, under Code & automation, Copilot, Cloud agent - enable and configure it there.
options.why: That is the documented path. Once configured, the agent is scoped to that repository and cannot operate outside it.

options.text: By adding a .github/agents/ directory - creating the directory is what enables the agent.
options.why: Custom agent files refine scope and capability within a repository, but they do not enable the cloud agent for it.

options.text: By adding the agent to the repository's CODEOWNERS file.
options.why: CODEOWNERS routes reviews. It does not enable or scope an agent.

takeaway: Repository scope is configured at the repository level; the agent then cannot operate outside that repository.

text: You are writing .github/workflows/agent-task.yml to run an agent nightly and on demand. Which combination of workflow elements is required for it to be a controlled execution path?

options.text: A trigger and a runner only - permissions are inherited automatically.
options.why: Inherited defaults are exactly what the guidance says to replace. Permissions should always be explicitly defined and minimized.

options.text: A trigger (for example workflow_dispatch plus schedule), an explicit permissions block, a job and runner, checkout, and authentication passed via env from secrets.
options.why: The workflow becomes the execution boundary: a defined trigger, a defined runner, a defined repository context, and only the permissions granted to that workflow. Authentication is supplied at runtime from secrets rather than embedded in the file.

options.text: A schedule trigger and a hard-coded personal access token in the run step.
options.why: Secrets must never appear in workflow YAML in plain text. They are injected at runtime through protected secret boundaries.

options.text: A pull_request trigger only, since agents should never run on a schedule.
options.why: Scheduled agent work - reporting, dependency checks, triage - is a normal and supported pattern.

takeaway: Invoking an agent in CI means wrapping it in a workflow with an explicit trigger, explicit minimal permissions, and runtime-injected credentials.

text: How does a GitHub Agentic Workflow differ structurally from a traditional GitHub Actions workflow?

options.text: It replaces GitHub Actions with a separate agent runtime.
options.why: Agentic workflows compile to a lock file that GitHub Actions executes. They augment CI/CD rather than replacing it.

options.text: It pairs frontmatter (triggers, permissions, tools, safe outputs) with Markdown that describes the intended outcome, and the agent works out the steps within those guardrails.
options.why: The Markdown expresses intent; the frontmatter defines the boundaries. That is the whole difference: traditional workflows specify every step deterministically, while agentic workflows describe outcomes and let the agent determine how, inside declared constraints.

options.text: It removes the need for permissions because the agent decides its own access.
options.why: The opposite - permissions are declared in frontmatter, and the model defaults to read-only tokens.

options.text: It runs only on self-hosted runners.
options.why: Runner choice is unrelated to the distinction.

takeaway: Agentic workflows: Markdown states the outcome, frontmatter states the guardrails, and it compiles to a lock file that Actions runs.

text: A team believes they can control which branch an agent works on by setting a field in the custom agent file. Are they right?

options.text: Yes - the branch field in the .agent.md file sets the working branch.
options.why: No such control exists in the agent file. Custom agents define applyTo, tools, and instructions.

options.text: No - branch-based scope is enforced by the execution context, not the custom agent. With a cloud agent you select a base branch and the system creates the working branch; in CI the workflow determines the branch.
options.why: Custom agents define what files they focus on, what actions they can perform, and how they behave - but not branch creation, pull request behavior, or execution isolation. Those come from the system executing the agent.

options.text: Yes - applyTo accepts branch patterns as well as file globs.
options.why: applyTo limits which files or directories the agent focuses on. It is a path filter, not a ref filter.

options.text: No - agents always work directly on the default branch.
options.why: The opposite is true: agents create a branch, change files there, and open a pull request against a base branch.

takeaway: Custom agents control focus and capability. Branch creation, PR behavior, and execution isolation belong to the execution context.

text: Which statement best describes how far the Copilot cloud agent goes on its own once it has finished working?

options.text: It creates a pull request and merges it once required checks pass.
options.why: Merging is never automatic here. Even where a PR exists, merge remains gated by policy and human decision.

options.text: It prepares changes on a separate branch for review; you decide whether to create a pull request, request updates, or discard the work.
options.why: The limits unit is explicit: the agent works on a separate branch and prepares changes for review, but does not finalize them. The final decision stays in human control.

options.text: It pushes directly to the default branch and opens an issue describing what it did.
options.why: Agents do not work directly on the default branch - branch-based isolation is a core safety mechanism.

options.text: It waits for a human to create the branch before it can make any change.
options.why: The agent creates its own working branch from the base branch you selected.

takeaway: The agent prepares; you dispose. Branch isolation plus a human decision point on the pull request is the safety model.

text: Which guardrails are part of the defense-in-depth model in GitHub Agentic Workflows? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Read-only tokens by default, so the agent inspects state without directly changing it
options.why: Yes. The default posture is read-only; writes go through a separate controlled path.

options.text: Safe outputs - the agent proposes actions and a separate gated step decides what is allowed
options.why: Yes. This creates an explicit boundary between reasoning and writing.

options.text: Zero secrets in the agent process, plus sandboxed containerized execution and network isolation with allowlisted egress
options.why: Yes. Keeping credentials out of the agent runtime and constraining the sandbox and network limits what a compromised or misled agent can reach.

options.text: Automatic merge of agent pull requests once threat detection passes
options.why: No. Threat detection scans proposed outputs before a write action is applied; it does not authorize a merge. Merge stays under policy and human control.

takeaway: Agentic workflow guardrails: read-only defaults, safe outputs, no secrets in the agent process, sandboxing, network allowlists, and output threat detection.

text: A workflow's CI secrets work fine, but the agent's runtime cannot see them. What principle explains this?

options.text: Secrets are only available on self-hosted runners.
options.why: Secret availability is about boundaries and scoping, not runner type.

options.text: The agent's runtime environment has its own secret boundary and does not automatically inherit repository CI secrets.
options.why: This is stated directly in the operations unit. Secrets should be injected at runtime into the components that need them, and scoped - for example by environment - to reduce exposure.

options.text: Secrets expire after 90 days, matching artifact retention.
options.why: Ninety days is the default retention for workflow logs and artifacts, not a secret lifetime.

options.text: Secrets can only be read by jobs with contents: write.
options.why: Secret access is not derived from the contents permission.

takeaway: Do not assume the agent runtime inherits CI secrets. Inject at runtime, pass only to the component that needs it, and scope by environment.

text: An agent step fails midway, but the workflow keeps going and later steps commit half-finished work. Which change addresses the root problem?

options.text: Keep continue-on-error: false so a failing step stops the run instead of silently continuing, and log a meaningful error.
options.why: The error-handling guidance is to fail fast, log meaningfully, and prevent partial or inconsistent changes. Letting execution continue past a failure is what produced the half-finished commit.

options.text: Set continue-on-error: true so the workflow always reaches the cleanup step.
options.why: That is the opposite: it explicitly allows execution to continue after an error, which is how partial changes get committed.

options.text: Increase timeout-minutes so the step has more time to recover.
options.why: The step failed, it did not run out of time. More time changes nothing.

options.text: Move the agent step to a separate workflow triggered by workflow_run.
options.why: Splitting workflows changes sequencing, not whether a failure halts execution.

takeaway: Fail fast, log meaningfully, and never let a failed step leave partial state behind.

text: Your safe-iteration policy needs a rule for what happens when the same required check keeps failing on an agent's pull request. Which policy matches the module's guidance?

options.text: Let the agent keep revising until the check passes - convergence is the goal.
options.why: Unbounded iteration is how workflows flap. The published policy exists precisely to prevent infinite loops.

options.text: The agent may revise and re-run, but if the same required check fails twice, escalate to a human with what failed, what was attempted, what evidence exists, and a suggested next step.
options.why: This is the safe-iteration policy: bounded retries plus a defined escalation threshold, and an escalation payload that makes the handoff actionable rather than just a notification.

options.text: Escalate on the first failure so a human always sees it.
options.why: That trades one problem for another - a human interrupted by every transient failure will stop reading escalations.

options.text: Disable the failing check so the pull request can proceed.
options.why: Removing a required check is a governance-drift move. Treat renaming or removing required checks as high risk.

takeaway: Bounded retries plus a clear escalation threshold - and escalate with failure, attempts, evidence, and a suggested next step.

text: Which pair correctly separates rollback that GitHub gives you for free from rollback you have to perform deliberately?

options.text: Free: branch isolation and pull request review before merge. Deliberate: closing or discarding the PR, or reverting commits after a merge.
options.why: Branch isolation plus pre-merge review means unmerged agent work never touched the main codebase - rollback is the default state. Once merged, you must act: revert the commits. Before merge, discarding the PR is the cheap path.

options.text: Free: reverting merged commits. Deliberate: creating a branch.
options.why: Reverting a merge is a deliberate corrective action, and branch creation is part of the normal agent flow.

options.text: Free: environment approvals. Deliberate: required status checks.
options.why: Neither is a rollback mechanism; both are gates that prevent the change rather than undo it.

options.text: Free: workflow re-runs. Deliberate: artifact deletion.
options.why: Re-running a workflow does not undo a change, and deleting artifacts destroys evidence rather than reversing code.

takeaway: Branch isolation plus pre-merge review is rollback by default. Post-merge, rollback means an explicit revert - which is why small, scoped PRs matter.

text: Which mechanisms implement an escalation path for an agent that cannot complete its task? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Requiring pull request review before the change can proceed
options.why: Yes. Review is the built-in handoff point where a human takes over a decision the agent could not make.

options.text: Automatically assigning reviewers - for example via CODEOWNERS on the affected paths
options.why: Yes. Automatic assignment routes the escalation to people with the right context instead of leaving it unowned.

options.text: A workflow step that notifies maintainers when the agent reports it is blocked
options.why: Yes. Notification steps make escalation active rather than relying on someone noticing a stalled PR.

options.text: Increasing the retry count until the agent eventually succeeds
options.why: No. Unbounded retries are the alternative to escalation, not a form of it - and for security failures the guidance is explicitly to investigate rather than retry.

takeaway: Escalation is a designed route to a human: required review, automatic reviewer assignment, and active notification - not more retries.

text: A team notices that agent actions performed with GITHUB_TOKEN do not kick off further workflow runs, but the same actions using a GitHub App token do. What is the practical implication?

options.text: GITHUB_TOKEN is broken and should be replaced with an App token.
options.why: This is documented behavior, not a defect. Most actions taken with GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger additional workflow runs.

options.text: The GITHUB_TOKEN restriction helps prevent unintended loops; App tokens and PATs enable richer chaining but require deliberate design to avoid recursive execution.
options.why: The restriction is a loop guard. Other authentication methods can trigger further runs depending on configuration, which enables more flexible automation patterns but demands careful design to avoid recursion and runaway automation.

options.text: App tokens should never be used with agents.
options.why: They are legitimate when you actually need downstream workflows to fire; you just have to design for it.

options.text: Workflow chaining is impossible on GitHub.
options.why: workflow_run triggers and other patterns support chaining explicitly.

takeaway: GITHUB_TOKEN's non-triggering behavior is a deliberate loop guard. If you switch to App tokens or PATs, design against recursive execution.

text: In the Agentic Workflows exercise, the workflow gathers information from Mona's notes, the GitHub Blog, and the Changelog and then proposes website updates. How does it deliver those updates?

options.text: It commits directly to the default branch so the site stays current.
options.why: Direct-to-default is the pattern the whole exercise is designed to avoid. Proposed changes must be reviewable before they land.

options.text: It opens a pull request containing the proposed changes and a summary of the sources used, so a human can review before merging.
options.why: The exercise's expected outcome is a pull request with proposed website updates and a clear summary of sources and reasoning - proposals reviewed by a human, not applied automatically.

options.text: It emails maintainers a diff for manual application.
options.why: That takes the work off-platform and loses the review surface, the checks, and the audit trail.

options.text: It writes the updates into a workflow artifact only, with no repository change proposed.
options.why: An artifact alone would not propose the change. The exercise explicitly produces a PR.

takeaway: Agentic workflows land their work as reviewable pull requests with a summary of sources - proposal first, human decision second.
